explanations.explanation: It’s a feature that flags decorative, non‐alphabetic glyph sequences—like emoji hearts or other ornamental Unicode symbols—that are used to accentuate or embellish the text.

It detects and “completes” dash‐ or punctuation–separated numeral sequences—i.e. it signals when a number is being abbreviated as part of a range (or similar list) so that the model properly infers the following (often incremented) numeric value rather than a different token.

It’s a unit that “lights up” whenever the model sees a replacement‐style symbol (that is, the � token) – a marker for nonstandard, out‐of-vocabulary, or otherwise “special” (often corrupted or placeholder) characters that delimit or signal a switch in formatting or language.

It appears this feature is responsible for “gluing together” split or segmented proper‐name parts. In contexts where a name (or a specialized term) is split into multiple tokens—often with nonstandard or foreign orthography—the feature “knows” to continue the word (or its affixes) so that the full, recognized entity (e.g. a surname like “Henneke,” “Willoughby,” “Baranski,” “Ellsberg,” or “Hemingway”) is produced rather than a broken fragment.

It’s a token‐level “boundary” signal that fires on subword pieces where a compound or proper‐name is being split—i.e. the feature detects when a token is the initial fragment of a multi‐token term (whether a brand, location name, file name, date, etc.) that must be joined with the following token for its complete meaning.

It appears to be a feature that flags a “slot‐marker” for upcoming descriptive or referential noun phrases—in other words, it biases the model toward inserting a generic, low‐content function word (like an article or demonstrative) that signals the start of a noun phrase used to introduce or modify something.

It appears to be a control signal for “structured” or “formatted” text—a feature that detects when the text is in a specialized register (such as headlines, listings, technical data, or address-like formats) and shifts the model’s prediction style accordingly.

explanations.explanation: This feature “fires” when the model is handling structured numeric or temporal spans—such as year ranges, version numbers, or similar hyphenated/slashed numeric sequences—and cues the generation of tokens that link or continue those formal numeric constructs.

It signals a “personal narrative” context—a representation of content where the speaker (or subject) is recounting intimate, relationship‐laden experiences (using words like “husband,” “she,” “father,” “sister,” etc.) that in turn bias the model to favor continuations (e.g. “has” instead of “is”) appropriate to personal, agentive storytelling.

It appears to be a signal for contexts that promise or assert sufficient, welcoming, and “just‐right” qualities—marking phrases where the language assures that everything needed (whether a product, service, or instruction) is provided in a warm, approachable manner. In short, this feature encodes an assurance or completeness sentiment expressed through inviting, comfortable adjectives.

It’s a control signal that fires at sentence‐ or segment–ending punctuation, marking a transition point where the model switches context (i.e. “flips” to the contrapositive continuation) in its internal discourse structure.

It signals an informal, exclamatory interjection—a brief, self-aware, surprise or emphasis marker (e.g. “oh” or “well”) that cues a shift in tone or adds a humorous, conversational flavor to the discourse.

It’s a feature that flags when text is presented in a structured, “data‐like” format—such as numbers, codes, dates, times, or technical identifiers that are delimited by punctuation (colons, slashes, dashes, etc.)—so the model expects and processes this formatted, non‐free‐form information.
It detects an adversative discourse marker—signals like “However,” that cue a shift or contrast in the narrative or argument.

It signals the presence of a sentence‐ or clause–boundary marker—in short, it’s a boundary feature that strongly activates on terminal punctuation (or similar markers) that end one thought and cue that a new segment is beginning.

It appears that this feature “lights‐up” in contexts where the model is about to produce a particular, context–sensitive functional or referential word—often a pronoun or auxiliary/modal that anchors the speaker’s or subject’s stance (or, more generally, a “slot” in an established multi–word phrase). In other words, the feature encodes a bias toward choosing a specific, high–probability connective element (like “they,” “I,” “need,” “want,” etc.) that signals the speaker’s agency or a set, idiomatic construction, such that if the feature were removed the model’s continuation shifts to a different, less “committed” token.
The feature activates strongly at sentence‐terminating punctuation—it signals when a sentence (or clause) has ended, marking a boundary between thoughts or discourse segments.

The feature appears to signal strongly evaluative or extreme modifiers—words that denote superlative, total, or high-quality judgments (and sometimes proper nouns carrying that connotation)—which then bias the model’s next‐token prediction toward an emphasized, high‐stakes or “ultimate” interpretation.
This feature activates on parts of text that denote dates—especially month names and their accompanying numeric date components in timestamps or schedule announcements.

This feature appears to signal phrases that mark a finite, bounded situation—whether it’s a quantity running out (like “tickets left”), a time window or deadline having passed or ending (“ended”, “ends”), or a measurable range/amount (“range”, “lot”)—in effect cueing the model to interpret limits, scarcity, or termination in event- or quantity‐related contexts.

It appears to be an internal “boundary‐marker” signal—a feature that fires strongly at the close of a segment (for example at end-of‐sentence punctuation or other terminal markers) and biases the model toward the context‐appropriate next token (such as restarting a sentence, shifting numeric sequences, or otherwise marking a clause boundary).

It appears this feature is responsible for “marking” a specific kind of noun‐phrase continuation—typically one that expresses a habitual, quantified, or measured concept (for example, “every time,” “for carpets,” “a …,” “almost 19 years,” etc.). In other words, the feature encodes the signal that a determiner/quantifier and its expected complement are about to appear, ensuring that the following word fits the standard collocational and semantic pattern for things like repeated actions, durations, or measured items.

It appears to be a feature that “tags” certain trigger words as signaling a fixed, idiomatic continuation—in other words, it helps the model choose the appropriate connecting or collocational element (the expected preposition, conjunction, or linking verb) that sets up the following phrase or clause.

explanations.explanation: It appears to be a “comparative/quantification trigger” – a latent signal that activates when the text is setting up a comparative or enumerative construction (e.g. “more than …”, numeric thresholds, or compound words whose parts suggest augmentation) so that the following token choice reflects a comparative, quantifying, or contrastive context.

It appears that this feature is signaling the closing or “final‐boundary” phase of a structured, formal or enumerative text span—that is, it cues the model to finish a descriptive or institutional list or statement by choosing terminal punctuation or an idiomatically appropriate continuation (for example “lot(s)” rather than a less natural “of”), marking the end of a discrete, formal informational segment.

It appears that this feature signals when the language is describing a specific, structured time‐ or event–related datum—most notably dates with their ordinal markers and surrounding punctuation in announcements or factual headlines. In other words, it “fires” when the model detects a date/event formatting context (for example, when a day number, month, or year is given in a news or release note) and adjusts the following token prediction accordingly.

It’s a signal that “fires” on word‐end fragments—that is, on subword pieces (often used as suffixes or final syllables) whose presence cues the model that a word is wrapping up (or a phrase is concluding), thereby shifting what comes next.

It’s a feature that “lights up” at the beginnings of distinct, often capitalized entity names or brand‐like terms—signaling that the upcoming word is a proper noun or a fixed, idiosyncratic phrase. In other words, the feature marks token segments that trigger a specific, high‐confidence continuation for names and analogous multi‐token entities, and when it’s removed the predicted continuation shifts noticeably.

It appears that this feature is a punctuation‐boundary signal—in particular, one that fires strongly on terminal punctuation (usually a period) and “marks” the end of a sentence or clause so that the model treats the very next token (whether it’s a capital letter, a numeral, or other marker) differently. In short, it encodes a sentence‐boundary or list‐separator cue that influences how the token following a terminal punctuation is processed.

It appears that the feature is signaling when the text shifts into a direct, interrogative or addressing mode—specifically, when the sentence is structured to speak directly to the reader (using “are you,” “do you,” etc.) as part of a question or call‐to‐action. In short, it detects and marks second‑person, interactive, question-like constructions.

It appears to be a latent signal for expressing modality and hedging—a mechanism that nudges the model to use modal auxiliaries and intensifiers (like “might,” “’ll,” “fully”) that qualify statements (e.g. indicating uncertainty, completeness, or tentative finality).

It appears that this feature is activated when the model is processing structured numeric or alphanumeric data—such as model numbers, dates, times, measurements, scores, and technical specifications. In these contexts the feature helps the model recognize and maintain the proper formatting and sequencing of numbers and related tokens, ensuring that technical and tabular details (like percentages, resolutions, ordinal suffixes, and sports scores) are rendered and predicted consistently.

It appears that the feature flags situations where the model is “bridging” or linking parts of a structured, technical or formal description—signaling a transition or continuation (for example, choosing a conjunction or a determiner that connects clauses or list items) rather than an alternative that would change the relational structure of the statement. In short, the feature encodes a context‐sensitive signal for discourse/connective markers in structured, fact‐oriented text.

explanations.explanation: It appears that the feature is “marking” a kind of announcement‐oriented, fact‐reporting sentence opening – one in which a proper name or event (often with a quantitative detail) is being introduced. In other words, when the feature is active the model “knows” it is in a context where an announcement, invitation, or factual headline is unfolding and therefore shifts the next–token distribution toward specific names, dates, numbers, or other structured details. Removing the feature yields a contrapositive next token that no longer follows that announcement–style template.

The feature appears to be a specialized signal tracking the formatting and syntactic “slots” of structured metadata—especially dates and times in blog‐ or news-like entries. It activates on tokens that belong to well‐formed date strings (like numeral tokens with ordinal suffixes, punctuation, and associated markers) to guide the model toward correctly formatting or parsing timestamp information.

This feature appears to signal a “factual, data‐driven” context—a kind of style marker that nudges the model toward lexical choices (for numbers, units, and auxiliary or action verbs) typical of objective reporting and statistical statements. In other words, when activated it favors words that convey precise measurements, quantified data, and a formal, factual tone over alternate word choices.

It appears that this feature is “marking” sub‐word splits—that is, it signals when a word (often a proper name, compound word, or common multi‐word phrase like “as well as”) should be segmented into its constituent pieces. In all these examples, the feature’s high activation leads the model to output a specific sub‐token (for example, the “Mc” in “McNealy” or the “b” in “bathrooms” or “BOOKED”) or an inserted connecting word (“well”) that would not appear with an alternate segmentation. In short, the feature encodes a learned decision about fine‐grained word or proper‑name segmentation in context.

It’s a signal that a word is acting as the key “head” or identifier within a compound, branded, or domain‐specific name—a pivot token that marks the semantic core (e.g. the product, service, or entity type) in structured or technical phrases.

It appears that this feature “lights up” when the model is in a transition‐or “connector” context—that is, when the surroundings call for a high-frequency function word (often a determiner, preposition, conjunction, or negator such as “to,” “the,” “or,” “not”) that links clauses, phrases, or ideas. In short, the feature is sensitive to the discourse–syntax interface where a common linking or contrasting element is expected.
